subject: General / Air Law
learning_objective: Apply the head-on right-of-way rule.
question_text: When two aircraft are approaching head-on or approximately so and there is danger of collision, each shall

choices.label: C
choices.text: avoid the other by changing altitude.

explanation: In a head-on or near-head-on encounter with collision risk, each aircraft must alter heading to the right, so both pass on each other's left.

incorrect_answer_explanations.B: Turning left would keep the aircraft converging.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: No rule mandates an altitude change as the primary head-on avoidance action.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: Anti-collision lights aid visibility but are not the mandated avoidance manoeuvre.

regulation_reference: Canadian Aviation Regulations (CARs), right-of-way rules; exact section not independently re-verified this session.

subject: General / Air Law
learning_objective: State the category-based right-of-way exception applicable to gliders.
question_text: When two aircraft are on converging headings at approximately the same altitude, the aircraft that has the other on its right shall give way except that, gliders shall give way to
explanation: Under the category-based right-of-way hierarchy, gliders rank above airships and powered aircraft (including rotary wing) but below balloons; gliders must therefore give way only to balloons among these options.

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: Gliders have priority over rotary wing (powered) aircraft, not the reverse.
incorrect_answer_explanations.B: Gliders have priority over powered aeroplanes generally, including 'heavy' aeroplanes.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: Gliders have priority over airships in this hierarchy.

regulation_reference: Canadian Aviation Regulations (CARs), right-of-way category hierarchy; mirrors ICAO Annex 2.

subject: General / Air Law
learning_objective: Define controlled airspace.
question_text: "Controlled Airspace" means an airspace of defined dimensions within which

choices.label: A
choices.text: aircraft must proceed in accordance with a SCATANA clearance.

choices.label: B
choices.text: an Air Traffic Control (ATC) service is provided.

choices.label: C
choices.text: only aircraft equipped with functioning two-way radio may operate.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Control is provided for instrument flight rules (IFR) traffic only.

explanation: Controlled airspace is defined as airspace of defined dimensions within which an air traffic control service is provided.

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: SCATANA is an unrelated national security air-traffic-control plan, not the definition of controlled airspace.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: A two-way radio requirement is not part of the basic definition of controlled airspace (though it may be required to operate within specific controlled airspace classes).
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: ATC service in controlled airspace is not limited to IFR traffic only; VFR flights also receive services in controlled airspace.

subject: General / Air Law
learning_objective: State the registration/airworthiness/marking requirements for flying an aircraft in Canada.
question_text: Except for ultra-light aeroplanes, no person shall fly an aircraft in Canada unless

choices.label: B
choices.text: there is in force with respect to the aircraft a Certificate of Airworthiness or a Flight Permit.

choices.label: C
choices.text: its nationality and registration marks are affixed to the aircraft in a proper manner, and are clear and visible.

choices.label: D
choices.text: all of the above conditions are met.

explanation: All three conditions (registration, a valid Certificate of Airworthiness or Flight Permit, and properly affixed and visible nationality/registration marks) must be met for an aircraft (other than an ultra-light aeroplane) to be flown in Canada.

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: Registration alone is necessary but not sufficient; airworthiness documentation and marking requirements also apply.
incorrect_answer_explanations.B: A valid airworthiness document alone is necessary but not sufficient without registration and marking compliance.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: Proper marking alone is necessary but not sufficient without registration and airworthiness documentation.

regulation_reference: Canadian Aviation Regulations (CARs), aircraft registration/airworthiness/marking requirements.

subject: General / Air Law
learning_objective: State a fitness-for-duty restriction for glider flight crew members.
question_text: No person shall attempt to fly as a flight crew member of a glider if

choices.label: A
choices.text: less than five take-offs and landings have been completed in the preceding six months.

choices.label: B
choices.text: within the preceding 14 hours alcohol has been consumed.

choices.label: C
choices.text: experiencing a physical disability likely to prohibit immediate licence renewal.

choices.label: D
choices.text: less than five supervised take-offs and landings have been completed in the preceding six months.

explanation: A flight crew member must not fly while experiencing a physical disability likely to prevent them from meeting the medical standard for immediate licence renewal — a fitness-for-duty restriction distinct from recency-of-experience currency requirements.

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: Recency-of-experience figures are separate from this fitness-for-duty restriction and are not the rule being tested here.
incorrect_answer_explanations.B: The alcohol restriction period specified elsewhere in Canadian air law is a different (typically 12-hour, not 14-hour) figure and is not the rule tested by this specific question.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: The 'supervised' takeoffs/landings framing does not match the rule tested here.

regulation_reference: Canadian Aviation Regulations (CARs), flight crew fitness for duty.

subject: General / Air Law
learning_objective: State the minimum altitude over built-up areas.
question_text: Except when taking off from or landing at an airport or military aerodrome aircraft shall not be flown over the built-up areas of any city, town or other settlement or over an open-air assembly of persons except at an altitude that will permit in the event of an emergency, the landing of the aircraft without undue hazard to persons or to property on the surface; such altitude shall not in any case be less than . . . . . above the highest obstacle within a horizontal radius of two thousand feet from the aircraft. The correct entry to complete the blank space is
explanation: The minimum altitude over built-up areas or open-air assemblies is 1,000 feet above the highest obstacle within a 2,000-foot horizontal radius of the aircraft.

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: 500 feet understates the required minimum for built-up areas.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: 2,000 feet overstates the required minimum height figure (though it correctly matches the horizontal radius figure, which is a different quantity).
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: 3,000 feet overstates the required minimum for this rule.

regulation_reference: Canadian Aviation Regulations (CARs), minimum altitudes and distances.

learning_objective: Interpret a steady green light signal to an aircraft in flight.
question_text: A steady green light directed at an aircraft in flight means
explanation: A steady green light signal to an aircraft in flight means the aircraft is cleared to land.

incorrect_answer_explanations.B: 'Return for landing' corresponds to a different light signal (a series of green flashes).
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: Standard light signals do not include a specific 'cleared to base leg' signal.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: Standard light signals do not include a specific 'cleared for final' signal.

subject: General / Air Law
learning_objective: State the spoken distress signal.
question_text: In radio communications the signal which means that grave and imminent danger threatens and immediate assistance is required is the spoken phrase

choices.label: C
choices.text: PAN PAN, PAN PAN, PAN PAN.

explanation: 'MAYDAY, MAYDAY, MAYDAY' is the internationally recognized spoken distress signal indicating grave and imminent danger requiring immediate assistance.

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: 'SECURITE' is used for safety messages/navigational warnings, not distress.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: 'PAN PAN' signals an urgency condition (not immediately life-threatening), a lower severity than a MAYDAY distress call.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: 'ALERT' is not a standard radiotelephony distress phrase.

regulation_reference: AIM / ICAO radiotelephony phraseology, distress and urgency signals.

subject: General / Air Law
learning_objective: State the correct altimeter-setting procedure for a glider when the current setting is unavailable.
question_text: A glider is preparing for take-off from an aerodrome in the altimeter setting region. If the current altimeter setting is not available the altimeter shall be set to

choices.label: A
choices.text: the mean sea level pressure of the aerodrome.

explanation: When no current altimeter setting is available, the altimeter is set so that it reads the known elevation of the aerodrome.

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: The altimeter subscale is set with a pressure value, but the pilot achieves this indirectly by setting the KNOWN ELEVATION on the altitude readout, not by directly inputting a computed sea-level pressure figure.
incorrect_answer_explanations.B: The standard pressure setting (29.92 in. Hg) is used in the Standard Pressure Region, not as a substitute when a local setting is simply unavailable in the altimeter setting region.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: Setting the altimeter to read zero is not the correct procedure.

regulation_reference: Canadian Aviation Regulations (CARs), altimeter setting procedures.

learning_objective: State the minimum VFR flight visibility in a Control Area.
question_text: The minimum flight visibility for VFR flight in a Control Area is
explanation: The minimum flight visibility for VFR flight within a Control Area is 3 miles.

incorrect_answer_explanations.C: 2 miles understates the requirement.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: 1 mile understates the requirement for this airspace.

subject: General / Air Law
learning_objective: State the Aircraft Journey Log retention period.
question_text: Every owner of an aircraft shall preserve the Aircraft Journey Log for

choices.label: A
choices.text: one year after the date of the last entry in the log.

choices.label: B
choices.text: three years after the date of the last entry log.

choices.label: C
choices.text: as long as the aircraft has a valid Certificate of Airworthiness.

explanation: The Aircraft Journey Log must be preserved for one year after the date of the last entry.

incorrect_answer_explanations.B: Three years overstates the retention period for the Journey Log specifically.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: Retention is not tied to the currency of the Certificate of Airworthiness.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: Retention for the aircraft's entire life overstates the requirement for this specific record.

subject: General / Air Law
learning_objective: State the compliance requirement for an ATC instruction.
question_text: An Air Traffic Control "instruction"

choices.label: A
choices.text: is in effect "advice" provided by ATC and does not require acknowledgement by the pilot concerned.

choices.label: B
choices.text: is the same as an ATC "clearance" when issued by a Flight Service Section.

choices.label: C
choices.text: requires compliance when received unless aircraft safety is jeopardized.

choices.label: D
choices.text: must be "read back" in full to the controller and confirmed before becoming effective.

explanation: An ATC instruction is a directive requiring compliance, and the pilot must comply unless doing so would jeopardize the safety of the aircraft.

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: An instruction is a directive, not mere non-binding advice.
incorrect_answer_explanations.B: An instruction and a clearance are distinct ATC directive types, not interchangeable regardless of issuing facility.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: A full verbatim readback is not a universal requirement for every ATC instruction (specific readback requirements apply to certain instruction types).

regulation_reference: Canadian Aviation Regulations (CARs) / AIM, ATC instructions.

subject: General / Aeronautics
learning_objective: State the cause of wake turbulence.
question_text: Pilots are warned of the dangerous turbulence existing in the wake of large aeroplane in flight. The turbulence referred to is caused by

choices.label: D
choices.text: the vacuum created by aircraft passage.

explanation: Wake turbulence is caused by expanding, counter-rotating wingtip vortices generated as a lift-producing wing's high-pressure lower surface air spills around the wingtip toward the low-pressure upper surface.

incorrect_answer_explanations.B: Propeller/jet wash is a separate, more localized and rapidly dissipating hazard, not the primary source of the wake turbulence being warned about.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: Fuselage-displaced air is not the main source of significant wake turbulence.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: There is no 'vacuum' effect from aircraft passage causing this hazard; it is a lift-induced vortex phenomenon.

subject: General / Air Law
learning_objective: State who may authorize vehicle movement on an airport absent an ATC unit.
question_text: No person shall walk, drive or park any vehicle on any part of an airport used for the movement of aircraft, except in accordance with permission given by the appropriate ATC unit or, in the absence of any such unit, by

choices.label: B
choices.text: the local flying club or school manager.

explanation: In the absence of an ATC unit, the operator of the airport is the party authorized to grant permission for vehicle movement on the airport's movement area.

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: A guide or commissionnaire is not the designated authority for this permission.
incorrect_answer_explanations.B: A local flying club/school manager is not automatically the designated airport authority for this permission.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: Local police are not the designated routine authority for airport vehicle-movement permission (though they retain general enforcement authority).

subject: General / Human Factors
learning_objective: State an early symptom of hypoxia.
question_text: Pilots should be aware that an early symptom of hypoxia (lack of oxygen) is a sense of
explanation: An early, insidious symptom of hypoxia is a false sense of well-being (euphoria), which impairs judgement before other symptoms may be noticed.

incorrect_answer_explanations.B: Drowsiness can occur but is not the specific early symptom this question tests.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: Dizziness is a symptom of hypoxia but not the specific 'early' euphoric symptom emphasized here.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: Panic is not a typical early hypoxia symptom; the danger is precisely that hypoxia produces false well-being rather than alarm.

subject: General / Air Law
learning_objective: State the regulatory definition of 'day' in Canada.
question_text: ‘Day’ in Canada is defined as that period of time between

choices.label: B
choices.text: one hour before sunrise and one hour after sunset.

choices.label: C
choices.text: the end of morning civil twilight and the beginning of evening civil twilight.

choices.label: D
choices.text: the beginning of morning civil twilight and the end of evening civil twilight.

explanation: 'Day' is defined as the period from the beginning of morning civil twilight to the end of evening civil twilight.

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: Sunrise-to-sunset omits the civil twilight margin included in the regulatory definition.
incorrect_answer_explanations.B: A fixed one-hour offset is not the regulatory basis for this definition; it is tied to civil twilight.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: This reverses the twilight boundary relative to the correct definition.

subject: General / Air Law
learning_objective: State the conditions required for a glider to fly within Class C airspace.
question_text: Unless authorized by ATC, no person shall fly a glider within Class C airspace unless

choices.label: A
choices.text: the pilot receives and acknowledges a VFR clearance to do so.

choices.label: B
choices.text: the ground visibility is at least 3 miles.

choices.label: C
choices.text: the pilot maintains a listening watch on an appropriate radio frequency.

choices.label: D
choices.text: all of the above conditions are met.

explanation: All three conditions — an acknowledged VFR clearance, at least 3 miles ground visibility, and maintaining a listening watch — must be satisfied for a glider to operate within Class C airspace absent other ATC authorization.

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: A clearance alone is not sufficient without also meeting the visibility and listening-watch conditions.
incorrect_answer_explanations.B: Visibility alone is not sufficient without a clearance and listening watch.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: A listening watch alone is not sufficient without a clearance and the visibility minimum.

regulation_reference: Canadian Aviation Regulations (CARs), Class C airspace operating rules for gliders.

subject: General / Air Law
learning_objective: State when a glider pilot is required to file a flight plan or itinerary.
question_text: The filing of a flight plan or itinerary is only required when a glider pilot plans to proceed

choices.label: B
choices.text: to an altitude of more than 5,000 feet.

choices.label: D
choices.text: more than 25 NM from departure point.

explanation: A glider pilot is required to file a flight plan or itinerary when planning to proceed more than 25 nautical miles from the point of departure.

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: Conducting aerobatic flight is not, by itself, the trigger for the flight plan/itinerary filing requirement.
incorrect_answer_explanations.B: Altitude alone is not the trigger for this requirement.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: Carrying passengers alone is not the specific trigger for this filing requirement.

regulation_reference: Canadian Aviation Regulations (CARs), flight plan/itinerary requirements for gliders.

subject: General / Air Law
learning_objective: State the oxygen requirement for a glider pilot-in-command at high cabin pressure altitudes.
question_text: The pilot-in-command of a glider shall not fly at cabin pressure altitudes between 13,000 and 15,000 feet above MSL

choices.label: A
choices.text: unless continuously wearing and using oxygen masks supplying oxygen.

choices.label: B
choices.text: for more than 30 minutes, unless oxygen masks and a supply of oxygen is available.

choices.label: C
choices.text: unless passengers are continuously wearing and using oxygen masks supplying oxygen.

choices.label: D
choices.text: for more than 45 minutes, unless oxygen masks and a supply of oxygen is available.

explanation: At cabin pressure altitudes between 13,000 and 15,000 feet, the pilot-in-command must continuously wear and use an oxygen mask supplying oxygen.

incorrect_answer_explanations.B: This altitude band requires continuous oxygen use by the PIC, not a time-limited allowance.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: The continuous-use requirement applies to the pilot-in-command; this option incorrectly frames it as a passenger-only requirement.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: This altitude band requires continuous oxygen use, not a 45-minute allowance (a time-limited allowance applies at a different, lower altitude band under Canadian rules).

regulation_reference: Canadian Aviation Regulations (CARs), supplemental oxygen requirements.

subject: General / Aeronautics
learning_objective: State the reference direction of the total lift force on an aerofoil.
question_text: The total lift force acting on an aerofoil in flight is considered to act

choices.label: A
choices.text: upwards with reference to the earth's surface.

choices.label: B
choices.text: at 90º to the aircraft longitudinal axis.

choices.label: C
choices.text: at 90º to the average relative air flow.

choices.label: D
choices.text: at 90º to the average wing chord.

explanation: Total lift is defined as acting perpendicular (90 degrees) to the average relative airflow (relative wind), not to any fixed reference on the aircraft or the ground.

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: Lift is not defined relative to the earth's surface; that would make its direction description dependent on aircraft attitude in a way inconsistent with the standard aerodynamic definition.
incorrect_answer_explanations.B: Lift's reference is the relative airflow, not the aircraft's longitudinal axis.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: Lift's reference is the relative airflow, not the wing chord line directly (that reference instead defines angle of attack).

subject: General / Aeronautics
learning_objective: State the effect of an angle of attack increase at the point of stall.
question_text: At the point of stall an increase in the angle of attack results in

choices.label: D
choices.text: no effect on lift or drag.

explanation: Beyond the critical angle of attack (the stall point), further increasing angle of attack causes airflow separation, resulting in a decrease in lift and an increase in drag.

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: Below the stall, increasing angle of attack increases both lift and drag; beyond stall, lift decreases rather than continuing to increase.
incorrect_answer_explanations.B: Lift decreases (not increases) past the stall angle, while drag increases.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: Both lift and drag are significantly affected past the stall angle; there is not 'no effect.'

subject: General / Aeronautics
learning_objective: Define longitudinal stability in terms of the relevant aircraft axis.
question_text: Longitudinal stability refers to stability about the
explanation: Longitudinal (pitching) stability refers to stability about the lateral axis (the axis running wingtip to wingtip), governing nose-up/nose-down pitching motion.

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: Stability about the longitudinal axis (nose-to-tail) is roll (lateral) stability, not longitudinal (pitch) stability, despite the potentially confusing naming.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: Stability about the normal (vertical) axis is directional (yaw) stability, not longitudinal stability.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: 'Directional axis' is not a standard third axis name distinct from the normal/vertical axis used for yaw stability.

subject: General / Aeronautics
learning_objective: Compare the stalling speed of a glider in a coordinated turn to straight-and-level flight.
question_text: The stalling speed of a glider is

choices.label: A
choices.text: the same in coordinated turns as in straight and level flight.

choices.label: B
choices.text: inversely proportional to the wing loading.

choices.label: D
choices.text: greater in coordinated turns than in straight and level flight.

explanation: A coordinated turn increases the load factor (wing loading) needed to maintain the flight path, which increases stalling speed above its straight-and-level value.

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: The increased load factor in a turn changes the stalling speed; it is not the same as in level flight.
incorrect_answer_explanations.B: Stalling speed is directly (not inversely) related to increased load/wing loading in a turn.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: Stalling speed is directly affected by aerodynamic (load factor) loading, contrary to this option.

subject: General / Aeronautics
learning_objective: Define load factor.
question_text: The ratio of the total lift force acting on the wings of a glider during flight to the gross weight of the glider is known as the
explanation: Load factor is defined as the ratio of total lift force to the aircraft's gross weight.

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: Lift/drag ratio compares lift to drag, a measure of aerodynamic efficiency, not lift to weight.
incorrect_answer_explanations.B: Aspect ratio is a wing-geometry measure (span squared divided by area), unrelated to this lift/weight ratio.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: 'Power factor' is not the standard term for this ratio.

subject: General / Aeronautics
learning_objective: State how indicated stalling speed varies with altitude.
question_text: In straight and level flight at 6,000 feet ASL a glider stalls at 35 KT IAS. At what IAS will it stall in similar circumstances in the circuit at 1,000 feet ASL?
explanation: Indicated stalling speed does not change with altitude (it is true airspeed at the stall that increases with altitude, not indicated airspeed), so the glider will stall at the same 35 KT IAS at 1,000 feet as at 6,000 feet, in similar (weight/load-factor) circumstances.

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: 27 KT would imply indicated stalling speed decreases with altitude, which is incorrect.
incorrect_answer_explanations.B: 32 KT similarly incorrectly implies a change in indicated stalling speed with altitude.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: Indicated stalling speed does not increase with altitude; it remains essentially the same, all else being equal.

calculation_steps: Indicated airspeed at the stall is essentially independent of altitude for the same aircraft configuration and weight, so IAS at stall remains 35 KT at both altitudes.

subject: General / Towing Operations
learning_objective: State the signal a glider pilot uses to indicate an inability to release the tow rope.
question_text: While on tow a glider pilot is unable to release the tow rope. The signal to indicate this condition to the tow pilot is to

choices.label: A
choices.text: yaw the glider to the right and left in a series of skidding turns.

choices.label: B
choices.text: commence a series of "S" turns at normal tow position.

choices.label: C
choices.text: porpoise rapidly between high and low tow positions.

choices.label: D
choices.text: fly to the left of the tug and rock the glider's wings.

explanation: The standard signal for an inability to release the tow rope is for the glider pilot to move to a position to the left of the tow aircraft and rock the glider's wings, alerting the tow pilot to the problem.

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: Skidding yaw turns are not the standard signal for this condition.
incorrect_answer_explanations.B: 'S' turns at the normal tow position are not the standard signal for an inability-to-release condition.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: Porpoising between high and low tow position is not the standard signal for this specific condition.

regulation_reference: Standard glider aerotow emergency signal procedures.

subject: General / Towing Operations
learning_objective: Identify the component with which a 'weak link' is associated.
question_text: A "weak link" would most likely be associated with a
explanation: A 'weak link' is a deliberately weaker-strength component fitted into the tow line so it breaks before the tow-rope loads can damage the glider or tow aircraft, providing a controlled failure point.

incorrect_answer_explanations.B: Control cables are structural flight-control components, not fitted with a deliberately weak breakable link.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: Dive brakes (spoilers) are not associated with a weak-link safety device.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: Canopy latches are not associated with a weak-link device.

subject: General / Performance
learning_objective: Calculate forward distance travelled given a gliding ratio and altitude lost.
question_text: At a gliding ratio of 15:1, a glider descending 1,000 feet in still air will move forward a distance closest to
explanation: A gliding ratio of 15:1 means the glider travels 15 feet forward for every 1 foot of altitude lost. Over 1,000 feet of descent, this gives 15,000 feet of forward travel, which converts to approximately 2.5 nautical miles.

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: 2.2 NM understates the forward distance for a 15:1 glide ratio over 1,000 ft.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: 2.8 NM overstates the forward distance for this glide ratio and altitude loss.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: 3.1 NM overstates the forward distance for this glide ratio and altitude loss.

calculation_steps: Forward distance = gliding ratio x altitude lost = 15 x 1,000 ft = 15,000 ft. Convert to nautical miles: 15,000 ft / 6,076.12 ft/NM = 2.47 NM, approximately 2.5 NM.

subject: General / Aeronautics
learning_objective: State the purpose of wing spoilers in gliding.
question_text: In gliding, an important use of wing spoilers is to

choices.label: A
choices.text: increase the rate of descent at the same airspeed.

choices.label: C
choices.text: make safe approaches possible at slower airspeeds.

explanation: Spoilers disrupt airflow over the wing, reducing lift and increasing drag, which allows the pilot to increase the rate of descent at a given airspeed — a key tool for controlling the approach glide path in a glider, which has no engine power to manage descent rate.

incorrect_answer_explanations.B: Spoilers reduce lift and increase drag, not increase lift without a drag penalty.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: Spoilers are primarily used to manage descent rate/glide path, not specifically to enable slower approach airspeeds.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: Spoilers degrade (do not improve) the lift/drag ratio, which is precisely why they are useful for steepening the approach.

subject: General / Aeronautics
learning_objective: State the pitch correction needed to maintain IAS through a decreasing-headwind wind gradient.
question_text: To maintain an IAS of 50 KT during an approach through a wind gradient where the head wind is decreasing, the pilot should
explanation: As headwind decreases descending through a wind gradient, indicated airspeed tends to decay; pitching the nose down trades altitude for airspeed to maintain the target IAS through the shear layer.

incorrect_answer_explanations.B: Pitching nose up would further reduce airspeed, compounding the loss caused by the decreasing headwind.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: Applying spoilers increases descent rate/drag but does not directly correct for the airspeed loss from decreasing headwind in the way a pitch-down correction does.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: A constant pitch attitude would not compensate for the airspeed decay caused by the decreasing headwind component.

subject: General / Human Factors
learning_objective: Describe the illusion risk when turning from downwind to base leg in strong wind.
question_text: When turning from downwind to base leg for landing, a strong wind could cause a pilot to experience an illusion of
explanation: As groundspeed falls during a turn from downwind toward a more into-wind track, a pilot can experience an illusion that prompts an inappropriate skidding correction to the turn, similar to the well-documented downwind-turn illusion.

incorrect_answer_explanations.B: Side-slipping is not the standard illusion associated with this turn scenario.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: The known hazard is an illusion prompting a skid, not a sensation of overbanking per se.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: Groundspeed decreases, not increases, during this turn segment, and the illusion concerns the pilot's control response (skid), not a direct perception of groundspeed.
